questions.q: What question does the Chinchilla trade-off answer that single-axis scaling laws (Lesson 14) don't?
options: How to clean training data before tokenization
Which GPU vendor offers the cheapest FLOPs
Given a fixed compute budget, how should it be split between model size and dataset size
How to choose a tokenizer vocabulary size
questions.explain: Single-axis scaling laws show loss falls as N, D, or C grow independently. The Chinchilla question is the compute-optimal split between N and D for a fixed C.

questions.q: What methodological issue did Hoffmann et al. (2022) identify in earlier (Kaplan-era) guidance?
options: The earlier models were all trained on image data instead of text
The earlier fits used too much training data
The earlier researchers used the wrong programming language
Learning-rate schedules weren't properly tuned for each run's length, which biased the recommended split toward oversized models relative to their data
questions.explain: The original scaling-law fits didn't account for learning-rate schedules mismatched to run length, which skewed the recommended N/D split toward bigger models and less data.

questions.q: In the Chinchilla paper's headline comparison, why did the 70B-parameter Chinchilla outperform the 280B-parameter Gopher?
options: Gopher was trained on corrupted data
Chinchilla had access to more GPUs than Gopher
Chinchilla used a completely different transformer architecture
Chinchilla used the same compute budget as Gopher but split it toward far more training tokens per parameter
questions.explain: Chinchilla and Gopher used comparable compute budgets, but Chinchilla's smaller size paired with far more tokens (1.4T) hit a better point on the compute-optimal frontier.

questions.q: What is the widely cited compute-optimal rule of thumb from Chinchilla's fitted curves?
options: Token count should always equal parameter count squared
Roughly 20 tokens per parameter
Roughly 1000 tokens per parameter
Roughly 1 token per parameter
questions.explain: Hoffmann et al.'s fitted optimum works out to approximately 20 training tokens for every model parameter, for a fixed compute budget.

questions.q: Why do many open-weight models deliberately train smaller than the compute-optimal point, using more tokens per parameter than ~20x?
options: Because inference cost scales with parameter count, not training tokens, so a smaller 'overtrained' model is cheaper and faster to serve at scale even though training it costs more
Because compute-optimal models cannot be fine-tuned later
Because larger models cannot be quantized
Because compute-optimal training is illegal in some jurisdictions
questions.explain: Compute-optimal minimizes training-time loss only. Since inference cost depends on parameter count, teams often accept a higher training cost to ship a smaller, cheaper-to-serve model.
